indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B4.4.1.1 Demonstrate understanding of the concept of energy, its various forms, sources and how to transform and conserve it
indicator.objective: Identify the effect of heat on the change of state of substances

skills.description: Recognise that heating can change a substance from one state to another (e.g. solid to liquid, liquid to gas).
Identify everyday examples of melting caused by heat (e.g. candle wax, shea butter, ice).
Distinguish between evaporation (slow change of liquid to vapour) and boiling (fast change with bubbles when heated).
Recognise that cooling can change a gas back to a liquid (condensation) — e.g. vapour from boiling water changes to water droplets when cooled.
Explain simply that the amount of water decreases after boiling because some water changes to vapour.
Predict what will happen when heat is applied to or removed from a substance (e.g. shea butter in the sun, water in a fridge).

spec.difficultyPlan: 20 questions total — Difficulty 1: 5; Difficulty 2: 7; Difficulty 3: 5; Difficulty 4: 3.
misconceptions: Boiling destroys water; it disappears completely.
Melting and boiling are the same thing.
Evaporation only happens when water boils.
Condensation happens when water is heated.
When water boils, its amount stays exactly the same.

questions.stem: What happens to ice when it is left in the sun?
hints: Ice is a solid. What happens to it when warmed?
questions.explanation: Heat from the sun changes solid ice into liquid water. This is called melting.
questions.misconception: Ice disappears completely when it melts.

questions.stem: When a solid is heated enough, it can change into which state?
hints: Ice is a solid. What does it become when it melts?
questions.explanation: When a solid is heated, it melts into a liquid. If heated further, it can change into a gas.
questions.misconception: Heating a solid makes it harder.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of melting?
options: Shea butter becoming liquid in the sun
hints: Shea butter starts as a solid.
questions.explanation: Shea butter is solid at room temperature. When left in the sun, heat melts it into a liquid.
questions.misconception: Shea butter becomes hard in the sun.

questions.stem: What do we see when water is boiling?
questions.explanation: When water boils, bubbles form and steam (water vapour) rises. Boiling is a fast change from liquid to gas.
questions.misconception: Boiling makes water freeze.

questions.stem: What will happen if you put a piece of shea butter in the hot sun?
hints: Shea butter is a solid that melts easily.
questions.explanation: Shea butter is a solid fat. When placed in the hot sun, heat melts it into a liquid.
questions.misconception: Shea butter becomes harder in the sun.

questions.stem: A pupil holds a candle near a flame. The candle wax changes from solid to liquid. What is this process called?
questions.explanation: Melting is when heat changes a solid into a liquid. The candle wax melted because of the heat from the flame.
questions.misconception: Melting and boiling are the same thing.

questions.stem: When water is heated and turns into steam, what change of state has happened?
questions.explanation: When water turns into steam, it changes from a liquid to a gas. This is evaporation or boiling, depending on how fast it happens.
questions.misconception: Boiling destroys water; it disappears completely.

questions.stem: What is the difference between evaporation and boiling?
options: Evaporation is fast; boiling is slow
Evaporation happens slowly; boiling happens fast with bubbles
Evaporation and boiling are the same
hints: Wet clothes dry slowly — is that evaporation or boiling?
questions.explanation: Evaporation happens slowly (like wet clothes drying). Boiling happens fast with bubbles when water is very hot.
questions.misconception: Evaporation only happens when water boils.

questions.stem: Steam from a boiling pot touches a cold plate and forms water droplets. What is this process called?
hints: The droplets form on a cold surface.
questions.explanation: Condensation is the change from gas (vapour) to liquid (water droplets) when the gas is cooled.
questions.misconception: Condensation happens when water is heated.

questions.stem: Give one example of a solid that melts when heated.
hints: Think of something you put in the sun that turns to liquid.
questions.explanation: Ice, candle wax, shea butter, chocolate and butter all melt when heated.
questions.misconception: Only ice can melt.

questions.stem: Ama left a piece of ice on a plate in the sun. After some minutes, what will she see?
options: The ice will turn into water
The ice will turn into stone
questions.explanation: The heat from the sun melts the ice into liquid water.
questions.misconception: Ice does not change in the sun.

questions.stem: A pupil boiled a cup of water for a long time. What will be left in the cup?
hints: The vapour escapes into the air.
questions.explanation: When water boils, some of it changes to vapour and escapes into the air. So there is less water left in the cup.
questions.misconception: When water boils, its amount stays exactly the same.

questions.stem: Water droplets form on the inside of a cold bottle of water. What caused this?
options: Vapour from the air cooled and changed to water droplets
The water inside the bottle melted
hints: Vapour in the air touches a cold surface.
questions.explanation: Water vapour in the air cooled on contact with the cold bottle and changed into water droplets. This is condensation.
questions.misconception: Bottles sweat like people do.

questions.stem: What happens to water vapour when it cools?
answer: it changes into liquid water droplets
questions.explanation: When water vapour cools, it condenses and changes back into liquid water droplets.
questions.misconception: Vapour disappears when it cools.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares evaporation and boiling?
options: Evaporation happens only when water boils
Evaporation happens at the surface and is slow; boiling happens throughout the liquid and is fast
Evaporation and boiling are the same process
questions.explanation: Evaporation happens at the surface of a liquid and is slow. Boiling happens throughout the liquid, with bubbles, and is fast.
questions.misconception: Evaporation only happens when water boils.

questions.stem: A pupil says, 'Melting and boiling are the same process.' What is the best correction?
options: Melting is solid to liquid; boiling is liquid to gas
Melting is liquid to gas; boiling is solid to liquid
hints: What does ice become when heated?
What does water become when boiled?
questions.explanation: Melting changes a solid to a liquid. Boiling changes a liquid to a gas. They are different changes of state.
questions.misconception: Melting and boiling are the same thing.

questions.stem: Why does the amount of water in a pot decrease after boiling for a long time?
answer: because some water changes into vapour and escapes into the air
some water turns into vapour and goes into the air
the water evaporates and escapes as vapour
hints: What do you see rising from a boiling pot?
questions.explanation: Some of the water changes into water vapour and escapes into the air, so the amount of water left in the pot decreases.
questions.misconception: Water disappears completely when boiled.

questions.stem: A learner puts a cup of water in a fridge. What will likely happen to the water if the fridge is very cold?
options: It will turn into shea butter
hints: Very cold water changes into what solid?
questions.explanation: If the fridge is cold enough, the water loses heat and changes into ice (freezes).
questions.misconception: Cooling makes water hotter.

questions.stem: Explain why wet clothes dry even when the sun is not very hot.
answer: because water evaporates slowly from the clothes into the air
the water in the clothes evaporates into the air
hints: Does water need to boil to evaporate?
Wet clothes dry at room temperature.
questions.explanation: Wet clothes dry because water evaporates slowly from the cloth into the air. Boiling is not needed for evaporation to happen.
questions.misconception: Evaporation only happens when water boils.

questions.stem: A learner measured 200 ml of water and boiled it for a long time. After boiling, only 150 ml of water was left. How much water changed into vapour?
hints: Subtract the water left from the water at the start.
questions.explanation: 200 ml − 150 ml = 50 ml. So 50 ml of water changed into vapour and escaped into the air.
questions.misconception: Boiled water disappears completely.
